title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
authors: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi
abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

infographic.key_insight: A mixture of expert neural networks learns data-assimilated flow corrections, achieving axial-compressor predictions close to assimilation accuracy without requiring experimental input during prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learned forcing terms can improve baseline RANS predictions for turbomachinery flows while reducing reliance on experimental measurements during deployment.
method: Fuse experimental PIV with fixed-grid steady RANS and moving-grid hybrid RANS/LES using a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter.
Train neural networks on the enriched database to map local velocity, velocity gradients and turbulent viscosity to Navier–Stokes forcing terms.
Use a Mixture of Experts to combine learned corrections for different flow regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against experimental data, the Mixture of Experts shows consistently lower discrepancies than baseline RANS and accuracy very similar to the assimilation results.
infographic.watch_item: Individual neural models can produce blade-tip errors exceeding baseline RANS; the abstract does not establish generalization to other geometries or operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows

title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: Seunghyun Joo
abstract: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread and exploits the structure of flow-solver kernels: pure accumulations need no tape, the remaining intermediate values are recomputed rather than stored, and adjoint updates are atomic only where several threads reach the same memory. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models: a viscous Burgers residual, a two-dimensional advection-diffusion residual, a quasi-one-dimensional Euler residual and a Biot-Savart summation over point vortices. All generated derivatives agree with finite differences and pass adjoint dot-product tests to round-off, while the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. Compared with the compiler-based tool Clad under the same compiler, CuAD gives identical results at identical cost on the stencil kernels and is 16 to 470 times faster on the summation kernel because it stores no tape. A steady Burgers study shows that in single precision the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent once the condition number grows to $2.5\times10^{5}$, whereas the CuAD Jacobian keeps the error below $5\times10^{-5}$. Four applications complete the evaluation: adjoint fields of the Burgers shock, the sensitivity of a scalar sensor in a cellular vortex, the inverse design of a transonic nozzle whose area is recovered to $2\times10^{-8}$, and an unsteady adjoint of the roll-up of a vortex sheet over 400 time steps.

infographic.key_insight: CuAD generates tangent and adjoint CUDA kernels directly from source, enabling accurate GPU-based sensitivities without storing an intermediate-value tape.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GPU-native discrete adjoints can support aerodynamic optimization, inverse design and flow-data assimilation while avoiding finite-difference sensitivity errors.
method: Transform CUDA kernels into ordinary CUDA tangent and adjoint source.
Organize reverse mode around GPU threads, recomputing intermediates instead of storing a tape.
Use atomic adjoint updates only where multiple threads access the same memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four flow-model kernels, derivatives agreed with finite differences and passed adjoint dot-product tests to round-off; adjoints cost 2–6× primal execution, and CuAD was 16–470× faster than Clad on the summation kernel.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation covers simple flow-model kernels; scalability and compatibility with full production CFD solvers remain to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics

title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation
authors: Soyoung Kim, Tiezheng Tong, Yinuo Noah Yao
abstract: Lab-scale membrane distillation (MD) modules are commonly used for membrane characterization and developing empirical heat-transfer correlations. Entrance-induced flow structures can introduce geometry-specific effects into measured temperature polarization (TP) and heat transfer. However, the dependence of these effects on module geometry and flow condition remains unclear. We performed three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations of direct contact membrane distillation (DCMD) over inlet Reynolds numbers of $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}=10$-$1000$, focusing on side-chamber length and main-channel height. We discovered that counter-rotating streamwise vortices formed near the main-channel entrance across all geometries, but their downstream persistence increased with $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. At lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$, the vortices mostly decayed before mid-channel, while at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ they persisted farther downstream and produced pronounced spatial variations in TP. Increasing side-chamber length reduced the secondary-flow kinetic energy entering the main channel, and generally strengthened TP, whereas increasing main-channel height reduced the bulk velocity and streamwise kinetic energy, resulting in a thicker thermal boundary layer and stronger TP. For most geometries, the deviation from the straight-channel baseline changed from stronger TP at lower $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$ to weaker TP at higher $\Re_{\mathrm{in}}$. Entrance effects therefore vary in both magnitude and direction with operating condition and cannot be represented by a constant correction across the Reynolds-number range.

infographic.key_insight: Entrance-generated vortices create geometry-specific temperature-polarization bias whose magnitude and direction change with inlet Reynolds number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lab-scale membrane characterization and heat-transfer correlations must account for entrance geometry and flow conditions rather than apply a constant correction.
method: Performed 3D CFD simulations of direct contact membrane distillation.
Varied inlet Reynolds number from 10 to 1000.
Examined side-chamber length and main-channel height against a straight-channel baseline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations found entrance vortices across all geometries, with greater downstream persistence at higher Reynolds numbers; most geometries shifted from stronger polarization than the baseline at low Reynolds numbers to weaker polarization at high Reynolds numbers.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational results without experimental validation, so transfer to other module designs requires verification.
infographic.paper_title: Reynolds-number-dependent entrance bias in temperature polarization of lab-scale membrane distillation

title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction
authors: Biswanath Barman, Rajendra K. Ray
abstract: Reconstructing flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements becomes particularly challenging when data are completely absent from dynamically critical regions, such as the vortex-formation region of a wake. Conventional interpolation and numerical reconstruction methods generally require sufficient spatial or boundary information, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can also face difficulties when sparse and noisy observations provide little or no supervision in the region of interest. To address this gap, we propose a Fourier-feature-embedded complex-valued physics-informed convolutional residual network (FCV-PICRN) for sparse, gappy, and noisy flow-field reconstruction. The framework integrates Fourier features for oscillatory and multiscale structures, complex-valued representations for coupled amplitude--phase learning, and convolutional residual blocks constrained by the Navier--Stokes equations. The method is first verified using the Taylor--Green vortex at $Re=100$ and then evaluated for the cylinder wake at $Re=100$. Three severe missing-data configurations are imposed in the dynamically sensitive wake: a large hole, a large truncation, and a plus-shaped gap extending in both streamwise and transverse directions. These gaps are further combined with additive Gaussian and multiplicative speckle noise. Despite having no supervised velocity data inside the excluded regions, FCV-PICRN reconstructs velocity, pressure, and vorticity with high structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and remains robust under Gaussian noise up to $20\%$. Finally, for forced two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence with $5\%$ Gaussian noise, FCV-PICRN yields lower reconstruction errors than a conventional PINN. These results demonstrate robust physics-informed reconstruction of severely incomplete and noisy flows across laminar and turbulent regimes.

infographic.key_insight: FCV-PICRN reconstructs flow structures inside unsupervised gaps by combining Fourier features, complex-valued learning, and Navier–Stokes constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help recover velocity, pressure, and vorticity from incomplete, noisy flow measurements when sensors miss dynamically important regions.
method: Fourier features encode oscillatory and multiscale flow structures.
Complex-valued representations support coupled amplitude–phase learning.
Convolutional residual blocks enforce Navier–Stokes physics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests cover Taylor–Green and cylinder-wake flows at Re=100, three severe wake-gap geometries, Gaussian and speckle noise, and forced 2D Kolmogorov turbulence, where reconstruction errors were lower than a conventional PINN with 5% Gaussian noise.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to the reported 2D cases; performance on 3D, higher-Reynolds-number flows and computational cost remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction

title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
authors: Prabakaran Rajamanickam
abstract: Stagnation curves of arbitrary shape (zeros of $\mathbf v(\mathbf x,t)$) are non-generic yet common; we derive their motion. Differentiating $\mathbf v=\mathbf0$ gives $\mathbf L\mathbf U=-\mathbf a$ ($\mathbf U$ curve velocity, $\mathbf a=\mathbf v_t$, $\mathbf L=\nabla\mathbf v$ kills tangent, acts on normal plane via $2\times2$ block $\mathbf K$); dynamics enters only via $\mathbf a$. Normal velocity: $-\mathbf K^{-1}$ times normal $\mathbf a$; tangential solvability: scalar condition $Σ=0$ per point ($Σ$: part of $\mathbf a$ outside range $\mathbf L$). Potential flow: $\mathbf K$ is strain rate, normal velocity pressure gradient over principal strain rate $ε$, persistence needs uniform pressure on it. Stokes flow: tangential vorticity enters $\mathbf K$ (centre lines), $Σ$ involves normal vorticity. Navier-Stokes: $Σ$ set by instantaneous flow via nonlocal pressure, viscosity. If $Σ\ne0$, line becomes, to first order in $t$, isolated points at zeros of $Σ$ (critical points of $\varphi_t$ if potential; maybe none in Stokes flow: loops vanish). Symmetry (line an orbit of rigid-motion group, no velocity along it) suffices for persistence, not necessary: flows steady in rigidly moving frame have $Σ\equiv0$. Incompressibility enters via $\mathrm{tr}\mathbf K=0$; for inviscid irrotational homentropic compressible flow, line dilatation is $\varphi_{tt}/c^2$, so lines can be nodes, persistence needs uniform enthalpy, singular $\mathbf K$ arises at ordinary points, acoustic standing waves give exact examples (node line breaking into alternating sinks, saddles); also degenerate $\mathbf K$ (pairs born at distance $O(\sqrt t)$), curvature, torsion evolution, closure for moving-singularity-driven flows, helical and elliptically conical stagnation-point flow, exact Navier-Stokes example: saddle, centre lines split into four points per period.

infographic.key_insight: Stagnation lines persist only when the local flow acceleration satisfies a compatibility condition; otherwise, they generally break into isolated stagnation points.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can help track the motion and breakup of zero-velocity structures in simulated viscous, inviscid and compressible flows.
method: Differentiate the zero-velocity condition to relate line motion to local acceleration and the velocity gradient.
Invert the normal-plane gradient block to obtain normal motion, and test a scalar compatibility condition for persistence.
Specialize the theory to potential, Stokes, Navier–Stokes and compressible flows.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical results and exact examples, including acoustic-wave breakup and Navier–Stokes lines splitting into four points per period, rather than empirical validation.
infographic.watch_item: The normal-velocity formula requires an invertible normal-plane gradient block; degenerate points need separate analysis, and generic breakup is described only to first order in time.
infographic.paper_title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows

title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades
authors: Hao Hao, Antonis Sergis, Maria N. Charalambides, Alex M. K. P. Taylor, Yannis Hardalupas
abstract: The impact of droplets, such as rain and sea sprays, on wind turbine blade surfaces can cause severe damage through leading-edge erosion (LEE). Current industrial practice has largely relied on empirical fatigue models to predict damage progression and guide maintenance. However, an important limitation of existing models is the assumption on ideal impact conditions, including perfectly spherical droplet and normal incidence, which rarely occur in reality. This study develops a fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model that couples incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element (FE) analysis of blade materials. Using this framework, we investigate the impact dynamics of droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations. The results reveal a positive correlation between the peak impact pressure, the influential area at the pressure peak, and the peak impact force. In contrast, the time of peak force scales inversely due to momentum conservation. From these findings, we propose a $\textit{universal scaling law}$ that relates all key impact loadings to the simple parameter of the droplet $\textit{projection area}$, which can be determined solely from the initial droplet geometry and orientation. This law provides a predictive framework for impact loading dynamics of non-ideal shapes, offering new insights into the mechanisms of LEE and improving the accuracy of erosion predictions for wind turbine blades.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed universal scaling law links droplet projection area to key impact loads, capturing the influence of initial shape and orientation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for non-spherical droplet impacts could improve wind turbine leading-edge erosion predictions and maintenance planning.
method: Couple incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element analysis of blade materials.
Investigate impact dynamics across arbitrary droplet shapes and orientations.
Relate impact loading metrics to initial droplet projection area.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show positively correlated peak pressure, loaded area at peak pressure, and peak force, while peak-force timing scales inversely; the abstract reports no quantitative errors or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed law needs validation across realistic rain and sea-spray conditions before use in erosion-life predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades

title: Fractal forcing of turbulence by settling particles
authors: Simone Tandurella, Alessandro Chiarini, Marco Edoardo Rosti
abstract: The settling of particles in a fluid medium can trigger complex collective dynamics, dramatically affecting the distribution of energy across flow scales. In this work we present the first fully-resolved observations of the turbulence induced by large particle structures, also known as cluster-induced-turbulence (CIT), obtained through particle-resolved direct numerical simulations at high volume fractions and density ratios in large domains. We find that particles arrange in macroscopic fractal structures, exciting turbulent fluctuations at scales much larger than the individual constituents. By virtue of their fractal nature, these clusters force the continuous-phase in a multiscale, self-similar way. We further show that these cluster-driven, vertically decorrelated fluctuations at large scales coexist with, but are fundamentally distinct from, the established particle-driven high-wavenumber scaling. Beyond unveiling a different form of clustering in particle-settling, these results highlight a naturally arising, self-assembling path to fractal-generated turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Settling particles self-organize into macroscopic fractal clusters that drive multiscale turbulence far beyond individual particle sizes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These findings could inform sedimentation and particle-laden flow models by distinguishing cluster-scale turbulence from particle-scale forcing.
method: Particle-resolved direct numerical simulations of settling particles.
Large domains with high particle volume fractions and density ratios.
Analysis of particle clustering and scale-dependent fluid fluctuations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations reveal large-scale, vertically decorrelated cluster-driven fluctuations coexisting with distinct particle-driven high-wavenumber scaling.
infographic.watch_item: Generality beyond the simulated high-volume-fraction, high-density-ratio conditions requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Fractal forcing of turbulence by settling particles

title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics
authors: Sangwon Park, Vinod Ramakrishnan, Arturo Machado Burgos, Andres Goza, Kathryn H. Matlack
abstract: Phononic materials (PMs) have emerged as a promising candidate to passively and beneficially interact with unsteady flows. However, their fluid-structure interaction (FSI) with separated flows exhibiting sustained periodic vortex shedding remains completely unexplored. In this study, we use a high-fidelity immersed boundary method to investigate the strongly coupled, nonlinear FSI dynamics of vortex shedding from a fully separated flow over a flat plate, with an embedded PM subsurface (PSub) modeled as a grounded diatomic chain driving a compliant section on the flat plate. We probe the dependence of the coupled system dynamics on two parameters: (1) the PSub chordwise position, which sets its spatial relationship to the flow structure, and (2) the rate of growth of the resonant displacement amplitude of a PSub, a behavioral parameter identified as a key driving parameter in PSub interaction with latent vortex shedding in prior work. Simulation results show that these two parameters drive clear and systematic changes to the limit-cycle vortex shedding. The PSub chordwise position determines the limit cycle PM-FSI dynamics, which can be classified into four distinct regimes as a function of position, ranging from substantial amplification to strong attenuation of lift and drag oscillation amplitudes in the limit cycle. Results reveal a configuration that reduces lift oscillation amplitude by over 30% and drag oscillation amplitude by over 50% with less than 0.5% change in mean lift and drag. Displacement amplitude envelope primarily governs transient responsiveness toward the limit cycle, where its influence also depends on the chordwise position. We analyze characteristic frequencies, the phase relationship between PSub displacement and lift, and unsteady and mean flow fields of the vortex-shedding process to explain mechanisms by which the PM modifies the flow.

infographic.key_insight: Positioning a passive phononic subsurface beneath a separated flat-plate flow can shift sustained vortex shedding from amplification to strong attenuation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A favorable configuration reduced lift oscillation amplitude by over 30% and drag oscillation amplitude by over 50%, with less than 0.5% change in mean lift and drag.
method: Simulated strongly coupled, nonlinear fluid–structure interaction using a high-fidelity immersed boundary method.
Modeled the phononic subsurface as a grounded diatomic chain driving a compliant plate section.
Varied chordwise position and resonant displacement-amplitude growth rate; analyzed frequencies, phase relationships, and flow fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations identified four position-dependent limit-cycle regimes, while displacement-amplitude growth primarily affected transient responsiveness in a position-dependent manner.
infographic.watch_item: Placement requires careful tuning: some positions amplify oscillations, and the abstract provides simulation rather than experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Interaction of Sustained Vortex Shedding with a Phononic Subsurface: Effect of Positioning and Resonant Characteristics

title: Yielding-dependent Taylor dispersion in electrokinetic-magnetohydrodynamic Casson microflows
authors: Nanda Poddar, Debabrata Das, Suman Chakraborty
abstract: Longitudinal dispersion in a yielding fluid depends on the velocity distribution and on how the flow is maintained. We study a neutral tracer in pressure-assisted electrokinetic and magnetohydrodynamic flow of a Casson fluid through a slit microchannel. The nonlinear stress and velocity equations determine the yielded layers, the unyielded core and the axial flow. Mei's multiple-scale homogenization of the advection-diffusion equation then separates transverse relaxation, mean drift and longitudinal spreading, yielding the Taylor-Aris auxiliary problem and effective diffusivity. An exact pressure-driven solution gives cubic decay of the mean velocity and eighth-power decay of the dispersion enhancement near flow arrest. Under fixed pressure and electrical forcing, increasing the yield parameter from $Y=0$ to $0.7$ moves the optimum Hartmann number from $Ha_p=0.696$ to $2.634$, while the corresponding normalized diffusivity decreases from $D_T^{\mathrm C}=1.454$ to $1.015$. At fixed mean throughput and $Ha_p=1$, the trend reverses: $D_T^{\mathrm C}$ increases from $1.000433$ to $1.002311$. The homogenized energy identity traces this difference to the velocity departure from the sectional mean, including that within the unyielded core. Analytical limiting solutions, direct concentration calculations, numerical convergence studies and a coupled Casson shear test support the reduced-flow predictions. An electrolyte-based dimensional assessment identifies the magnetic optima as theoretical forcing states for representative aqueous microchannels. These results are relevant to predicting longitudinal tracer spreading in microchannels carrying fluids with a yield stress, whether pressure or throughput is controlled.

infographic.key_insight: Yield stress suppresses Taylor dispersion under fixed pressure and electrical forcing but increases it at fixed mean throughput in Casson microflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting tracer spreading in yield-stress microfluidics requires accounting for whether pressure or throughput is controlled.
method: Solve nonlinear Casson stress and velocity equations for yielded layers and the unyielded core.
Apply multiple-scale homogenization to derive effective longitudinal diffusivity.
Use an energy identity to connect dispersion to velocity departures from the sectional mean.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical limits, direct concentration calculations and convergence tests support predictions: raising Y from 0 to 0.7 lowers optimum normalized diffusivity from 1.454 to 1.015 under fixed forcing, but raises it from 1.000433 to 1.002311 at fixed throughput and Ha_p = 1.
infographic.watch_item: The magnetic optima are theoretical forcing states for representative aqueous microchannels; practical magnetic-field feasibility needs assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Yielding-dependent Taylor dispersion in electrokinetic-magnetohydrodynamic Casson microflows

title: Bridging the Lattice Boltzmann Method and Moment Methods
authors: Jinhua Lu, Song Zhao, Pierre Sagaut, Nikolaus A. Adams
abstract: We derive discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) and identify the general moment closure shared by kinetic methods based on the discrete-velocity Boltzmann equation. This closure provides a route to correct lower-order dynamics without requiring accurate reconstruction of the higher-order moments, thereby substantially broadening the scope of existing closure strategies that seek increasingly accurate representations of these moments. These advances establish a unified moment framework bridging LBM and moment methods. The framework enables efficient simulations across all Knudsen regimes, overcoming the prohibitive complexity of existing moment methods at high Knudsen numbers. It further provides a common basis for integrating and extending key features of diverse kinetic methods.

infographic.key_insight: An exactly equivalent moment formulation of LBM reveals a shared kinetic closure that can correct lower-order dynamics without accurately reconstructing higher-order moments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to efficient flow simulations across Knudsen regimes while linking LBM with broader moment-method capabilities.
method: Derive discrete moment equations exactly equivalent to LBM.
Identify the general moment closure shared by discrete-velocity kinetic methods.
Use this closure to improve lower-order dynamics without requiring accurate higher-order moments.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical equivalence and claims efficiency across all Knudsen regimes, but provides no benchmark details or quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical accuracy, stability, and computational savings across Knudsen regimes require validation beyond the abstract's theoretical claims.
infographic.paper_title: Bridging the Lattice Boltzmann Method and Moment Methods

title: Probing Flow-Induced Chain Scission in Shear-Banding Wormlike Micelles
authors: Alfredo Scigliani, Samuel C. Grant, Hadi Mohammadigoushki
abstract: We investigate the microstructural dynamics of wormlike micellar (WLM) solutions based on CPyCl/NaSal/D\(_2\)O under shear flow using spatially resolved rheo-diffusion NMR, velocity-compensated diffusion measurements, and rheo-optical imaging in a Taylor--Couette geometry. Two viscoelastic systems were examined: a non-shear-banding WLM with a molar salt-surfactant concentration ratio of \(R=0.4\) and a shear-banding WLM with \(R=0.53\). Rheo-optical and velocity measurements confirm homogeneous flow for the non-shear-banding system and the coexistence of low- and high-shear bands within the stress-plateau regime for the shear-banding system. Despite the pronounced heterogeneity in velocity and shear rate associated with shear banding, the local surfactant self-diffusivity remains spatially uniform across the gap and throughout the stress-plateau regime. Furthermore, analysis of the mean-squared-displacement scaling reveals no measurable difference between the high- and low-shear bands. These results demonstrate that the micellar microstructure remains largely unchanged despite the formation of shear bands and provide direct experimental evidence that flow-induced micellar chain scission is not a dominant mechanism governing shear banding in this WLM system.

infographic.key_insight: Shear bands formed without measurable differences in local surfactant diffusion or displacement scaling, indicating that flow-induced micellar chain scission is not a dominant mechanism in this system.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Constitutive models for these wormlike micelles should not assume that shear banding necessarily entails substantial chain scission.
method: Compare non-shear-banding (R = 0.4) and shear-banding (R = 0.53) CPyCl/NaSal/D₂O solutions.
Measure local diffusion using spatially resolved rheo-diffusion NMR and velocity-compensated diffusion measurements.
Characterize flow bands using rheo-optical imaging and velocity measurements in Taylor–Couette geometry.
infographic.evidence_signal: Within the shear-banding stress plateau, local surfactant self-diffusivity remained spatially uniform, with no measurable difference in mean-squared-displacement scaling between low- and high-shear bands.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is specific to the tested formulations and measurement sensitivity; unchanged diffusion does not rule out all microstructural changes.
infographic.paper_title: Probing Flow-Induced Chain Scission in Shear-Banding Wormlike Micelles

title: Effects of Spanwise Curvature on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition in Görtler-driven Flows
authors: Andrew Welter, Ngoc Cuong Nguyen, Nicholas Webber, Mark Gragston, Jaime Peraire, Wesley Harris
abstract: The influence of spanwise convex curvature on hypersonic boundary-layer transition over a streamwise-concave surface is investigated using direct numerical simulation and Mach 7 experiments. Smooth doubly curved geometries with fixed streamwise concavity and increasing spanwise convex curvature isolate the effects of three-dimensional wall curvature on a centrifugally unstable boundary layer. Increasing spanwise curvature delays transition while preserving a Gortler-dominated route to breakdown. As spanwise curvature increases, the boundary layer thins, reducing the effective Görtler number and weakening centrifugal amplification of streamwise vortices. Consequently, growth of the primary Görtler instability is reduced, vortical structures remain closer to the wall, and secondary instability and turbulent breakdown shift downstream. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition confirms that low-frequency vortical dynamics remain dominant in controlling transition, with sinuous secondary instability of Görtler vortices providing the principal route to breakdown. Meanwhile, boundary-layer thinning modifies acoustic instability dynamics: the second Mack mode shifts to higher frequencies and higher-frequency supersonic disturbances become increasingly prominent near breakdown as spanwise curvature increases. These acoustic disturbances remain subdominant and do not replace the Görtler-sinuous mechanism as the primary transition pathway. Numerical and experimental results exhibit consistent trends in transition location, thermal-streak organisation and disturbance evolution, supporting a common physical interpretation. These findings demonstrate that spanwise convex curvature stabilises hypersonic Görtler-dominated boundary layers, primarily by suppressing centrifugal amplification and delaying secondary instability, while leaving the transition pathway qualitatively unchanged.

infographic.key_insight: Increasing spanwise convex curvature delays hypersonic boundary-layer transition by weakening centrifugal amplification while preserving the Görtler–sinuous breakdown pathway.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Spanwise curvature offers a potential geometry-based approach to delaying transition and managing aerodynamic heating on hypersonic surfaces.
method: Direct numerical simulations and Mach 7 experiments.
Doubly curved surfaces with fixed streamwise concavity and increasing spanwise convex curvature.
Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition to identify dominant disturbance dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations and experiments show consistent trends in transition location, thermal-streak organisation and disturbance evolution, with transition shifting downstream as spanwise curvature increases.
infographic.watch_item: Generalisability beyond the studied geometries and Mach 7 conditions remains unestablished; higher-frequency acoustic disturbances become more prominent but remain subdominant.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of Spanwise Curvature on Hypersonic Boundary Layer Transition in Görtler-driven Flows

title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators
authors: Yinghe Qi, Qutadah Rababah, Wei Guo
abstract: A sudden loss of vacuum in a superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerator drives warm gas into the evacuated beamline, where it propagates through interconnected SRF cavities cooled by liquid helium, causing surface contamination, intense heat deposition, and dangerous pressure buildup. Yet predicting how such a failure propagates through realistic multicell cavities has remained difficult because compressible gas dynamics, condensation and cryogenic heat transfer are strongly coupled. Here we develop and experimentally validate a multidimensional computational framework that resolves these processes, and apply it to a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity. We find that the repeated cell geometry produces staircase-like gas-front propagation, as impingement, recirculation and localized cryopumping strongly retard the bulk flow within each cell. Across a broad range of breach sizes, the cavity traversal time follows a robust power-law scaling with leakage area, providing quantitative guidance for the response time of beamline isolation and protection systems. The simulations also reveal a geometry-confined Mach disk whose position and size track the advancing gas front, suggesting that its acoustic emission could potentially enable rapid, non-invasive detection and localization of vacuum failures. These findings pave the way for a new generation of predictive diagnostics and protection strategies to safeguard large-scale superconducting accelerators.

infographic.key_insight: Repeated SRF cavity cells retard incoming gas in staircase-like steps, while cavity traversal time follows a robust power law with vacuum-breach area.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scaling law can guide isolation-system response times to limit contamination, heat deposition, and pressure buildup after vacuum loss.
method: Developed an experimentally validated multidimensional computational framework.
Coupled compressible gas dynamics, condensation, and cryogenic heat transfer.
Simulated a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity across a broad range of breach sizes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental validation and robust traversal-time scaling across simulated breach sizes, but gives no numerical errors or scaling exponent.
infographic.watch_item: Mach-disk acoustic detection remains a proposed diagnostic that requires validation before operational deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators

title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology
authors: Imanol García de Beristain, David Nieto Simavilla, Marco Ellero
abstract: We present GINNGER (GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for GEnerative Rheology), a framework for discovering thermodynamically admissible constitutive equations from microstructural flow data. Unlike existing approaches that learn constitutive operators, GINNGER reformulates constitutive discovery as the learning of the underlying thermodynamic generators from which constitutive equations emerge. Embedding the GENERIC formalism into the learning process restricts the search to constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction, eliminating the need to prescribe phenomenological constitutive equations a priori. A second conceptual advance is a spectral formulation of constitutive discovery in the intrinsic eigenspace of the polymer conformation tensor. This provides a kinematics-independent thermodynamic state space in which the thermodynamic generators depend only on the instantaneous microstructural state, while flow kinematics acts solely as an external driver transporting the system through this space. Consequently, data from shear, extensional, and mixed flows contribute to the discovery of a single constitutive model that generalizes across deformation protocols and flow geometries. By learning thermodynamic generators rather than high-dimensional constitutive operators, GINNGER substantially reduces the complexity of the discovery problem while preserving thermodynamic consistency, material objectivity, and physical interpretability by construction. The framework is validated using high-fidelity simulations, accurately reconstructing constitutive behavior and predicting complex flow fields across previously unseen geometries. GINNGER establishes a new paradigm for constitutive discovery by combining generative, spectral, and thermodynamically grounded learning within a unified framework for data-driven modeling of complex fluids.

infographic.key_insight: GINNGER learns thermodynamic generators rather than constitutive operators, yielding complex-fluid constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports transferable constitutive modeling for CFD across deformation protocols and flow geometries while preserving thermodynamic consistency and material objectivity.
method: Embed the GENERIC formalism into neural-network learning from microstructural flow data.
Represent thermodynamic state in the polymer conformation tensor’s intrinsic eigenspace.
Combine shear, extensional, and mixed-flow data to discover a single constitutive model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation against high-fidelity simulations, including accurate constitutive reconstruction and complex-flow predictions in previously unseen geometries.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative errors or computational costs, leaving practical accuracy and CFD integration overhead to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology

title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient
authors: Yu-Xuan Shi, Mingze Ma, Xi Chen
abstract: The adverse-pressure-gradient (APG) effect challenges the classical scaling of turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) over a flat plate, and it remains unclear whether outer-layer similarity holds across a wide range of APG strengths.We assemble a benchmark comprising the present direct numerical simulation of a suction--blowing-induced separation bubble and published profiles, spanning Clauser parameters $β_e=0.04$--$180$ and Reynolds numbers $Re_θ=530$--$19000$. Across this broad $(β_e,Re_θ)$ parameter range, existing APG normalizations do not simultaneously collapse the two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components, leaving open whether outer similarity persists. Instead of defining new scalings, we normalize each quantity by its value at a common location $y_s$. Results are shown using $y_s=0.5δ$, beyond the outer stress peaks. For each of the six quantities, the normalized profiles exhibit a common outer shape across the conditions, with collapse emerging for $y/δ\gtrsim0.2$ for the velocity defects and $y/δ\gtrsim0.4$ for the Reynolds stresses. The collapse-error analysis shows that outer self-similarity is retained over a broad range of $y_s$ within the outer region and is not restricted to $y_s=0.5δ$. Furthermore, explicit expressions are provided for the normalized outer profiles. These results support component-wise outer similarity under strong APGs and provide compact references for APG turbulence-model assessment and conditional profile reconstruction.

infographic.key_insight: Normalizing each velocity defect and Reynolds-stress component by its own value at a shared outer-layer location reveals component-wise outer similarity across strong adverse-pressure gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Explicit normalized outer profiles offer compact references for assessing APG turbulence models and conditionally reconstructing boundary-layer profiles.
method: Combine a new separation-bubble DNS with published turbulent boundary-layer profiles.
Normalize two mean-velocity defects and four Reynolds-stress components at y_s = 0.5δ.
Evaluate profile collapse and its sensitivity to the outer-layer reference location.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark spans β_e = 0.04–180 and Re_θ = 530–19,000, with collapse emerging at y/δ ≳ 0.2 for velocity defects and ≳ 0.4 for Reynolds stresses.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstrated similarity is component-wise and outer-layer-specific; profile reconstruction still requires each quantity's reference amplitude.
infographic.paper_title: Component-wise outer similarity of turbulent boundary layers with strong adverse-pressure gradient

title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem
authors: J. Yin, N. Harnik, E. Heifetz, J. Mak
abstract: A mechanistic interpretation for baroclinic normal mode instability with exponential growth is the interaction arising from Counter-propagating Rossby Waves (CRWs), where pairs of CRWs phase-lock and interfere constructively. On the other hand, an arbitrary initial condition can lead to finite transient growth as long as there is constructive interference. The present work investigates the characteristics of finite time transient instabilities and its description in terms of CRWs in a baroclinic system with asymmetric interaction, in contrast to usual settings where there is an inherent symmetry that leads to equal and opposite CRWs. A sloped Eady problem on a $f$-plane is considered here, which has the benefit that there are only two CRWs in the system, and the presence of a bottom topographic slope can be formulated in a such a way that only one of the CRW is affected and controlled by a single parameter representing the asymmetry, via modifying the bottom background potential vorticity gradient. We derive conditions where the instantaneous growths have key CRW properties that are independent of the asymmetry parameter for a reasonably general family of norms, and that the instability characteristic in the total energy norm is entirely independent of the asymmetry parameter. For finite time transient growth, the optimal initial condition is in some sense counter to that of the exponential growing normal mode: where the bottom slope is such that it is strengthening the bottom CRW, the normal mode has a larger bottom CRW, but the finite time optimal initial condition wants the bottom CRW to be weak instead, and vice-versa. While the results presented here are for the sloped Eady problem, the same results were also found for an analogous Phillips problem, and we speculate the instability characteristics may have origins in the underlying symmetries that are common to those two problems.

infographic.key_insight: Bottom-slope asymmetry changes the optimal initial balance of counter-propagating Rossby waves for finite-time growth, favoring the opposite amplitude bias to the exponentially growing normal mode.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The findings can inform stability analysis of rotating stratified flows, where normal-mode predictions alone may miss finite-time disturbance amplification.
method: Analyze two interacting Rossby waves in a sloped Eady model on an f-plane.
Control wave asymmetry through the bottom background potential-vorticity gradient.
Derive instantaneous-growth properties across a family of norms and examine finite-time optimal perturbations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports asymmetry-independent instantaneous-growth characteristics in the total-energy norm and analogous results in a Phillips model, but provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed symmetry-based explanation remains speculative, and applicability beyond the idealized models is not established.
infographic.paper_title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem

title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows
authors: Weiheng Zeng, Hao Wang, Jiaxin Zhu, Kun Wang, Tiegang Liu, Chengliang Feng
abstract: The physics-informed neural network (PINN) faces significant challenges when solving compressible multi-medium flows, including the inability to locate interface positions, poor approximation of discontinuities, and difficulty in handling high-pressure-ratio problems between media with large stiffness differences. To address these issues, we propose PINN with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition (PINN-LPCDD), a framework that incorporates the sharp interface method (SIM) into PINNs for solving compressible multi-medium flows. Firstly, we design separate sub-networks for each medium with learnable parameters to automatically learn interface positions, so that the domain decomposition is physically consistent, and the contact discontinuity at the interface is naturally sharp. Secondly, the Euler equations with artificial viscosity are solved to enhance robustness when handling problems involving shock waves. Lastly, the scaling invariance of the Euler equations is exploited to facilitate the solution of high pressure ratio problems. Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems demonstrate the acceptable accuracy of the proposed method in simulating multi-medium flows.

infographic.key_insight: PINN-LPCDD learns medium interfaces while using separate neural networks to preserve sharp contact discontinuities in compressible multi-medium flows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets shock-driven flows across dissimilar media, including high-pressure-ratio cases with large differences in material stiffness.
method: Use medium-specific subnetworks and learnable interface positions for physically consistent domain decomposition.
Solve Euler equations with artificial viscosity to improve shock-handling robustness.
Exploit Euler-equation scaling invariance to address high pressure ratios.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests on air–air, air–helium, air–water, and air–R22 problems show acceptable accuracy according to the abstract, which provides no quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Artificial-viscosity tuning and interface-learning stability warrant validation beyond the reported test cases.
infographic.paper_title: PINN-LPCDD: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition for Compressible Multi-Medium Flows

title: Pair-exchange dynamics of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence
authors: Jean-Mathieu Teissier, Wolf-Christian Müller
abstract: Nonlinear interactions in incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) and Navier-Stokes turbulence involve three spatial fluctuations conservatively exchanging, e.g., energy. The mathematical structure of a triad interaction does not allow to unambigously determine the specific contribution of each of the participating fluctuations to the resulting exchanges. Presently, only additional assumptions allow for the deconstruction of triad interactions into a sum of pair exchanges. This work proves that in incompressible MHD the simultaneous nonlinear transfer of cross-helicity sufficiently constrains the triad dynamics such that a mathematically unique pair-exchange representation of nonlinear energy and cross-helicity transfer is possible.

infographic.key_insight: In incompressible MHD turbulence, simultaneous cross-helicity transfer constrains triad dynamics enough to uniquely decompose nonlinear energy and cross-helicity transfers into pair exchanges.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This result provides a rigorous foundation for diagnosing energy-transfer pathways in incompressible MHD turbulence relevant to conducting-fluid and plasma simulations.
method: Analyze conservative nonlinear exchanges among three interacting spatial fluctuations.
Use simultaneous cross-helicity transfer to constrain the ambiguity in pairwise energy exchanges.
Prove uniqueness of the resulting pair-exchange representation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a mathematical uniqueness proof, with no numerical benchmarks or experimental validation described.
infographic.watch_item: The uniqueness result is stated for incompressible MHD and should not be assumed to extend to compressible MHD or Navier–Stokes turbulence.
infographic.paper_title: Pair-exchange dynamics of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence

title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions
authors: Miguel Sanchez-Gomez, Lucas Carmo, Matthew Churchfield, Jason Jonkman, Walter Musial
abstract: Tropical cyclones can produce extreme winds in the lowest portion of the boundary layer, posing high risks to critical energy infrastructure, including wind energy systems. This study evaluates the dynamic response of an idling wind turbine to turbulent inflow generated during the passage of a hurricane. We performed large-eddy simulations of Hurricane Laura (2020) at several grid resolutions -- coarse $(Δx=55.55\,{\rm m})$, intermediate $(Δx=25\,{\rm m})$, and fine $(Δx=10\,{\rm m})$ -- to investigate differences in mean flow characteristics and turbulence structures as the hurricane progresses across a virtual wind turbine location. The large-eddy simulation data served as direct inflow conditions for aeroelastic simulations to assess the turbine's response. Our results reveal significant differences in the mean wind and turbulent flow structures between the grid resolutions, leading to distinct impacts on the wind turbine's aeroelastic behavior. These findings emphasize the need for high-resolution inflow information to better predict extreme loads and inform the design of wind turbines in regions frequently affected by tropical cyclones. As a continuation of this work, Part II of this study will evaluate the turbine's response from different locations relative to the storm's trajectory and compare it with current wind turbine design practices.

infographic.key_insight: LES grid resolution changes predicted hurricane winds and turbulence, producing distinct aeroelastic responses in an idling wind turbine.
infographic.engineering_relevance: High-resolution hurricane inflow information can improve extreme-load predictions and support wind turbine design in cyclone-prone regions.
method: Simulate Hurricane Laura (2020) using large-eddy simulation.
Compare grid spacings of 55.55 m, 25 m, and 10 m.
Use LES inflow directly in aeroelastic simulations of an idling turbine.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three grid resolutions, the simulations showed significant differences in mean winds and turbulence structures, with corresponding differences in turbine response.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish grid convergence or quantify load differences; storm-relative location effects and comparisons with design practices are deferred to Part II.
infographic.paper_title: Hurricane Laura-induced loads on wind turbines -- Part I: High-fidelity modeling and sensitivity to turbulent inflow conditions

title: Hydrodynamics and propulsive efficiency of stern-sculling propulsion
authors: Gildas Roudaut, Benoit Augier, Marc Rabaud
abstract: Stern-sculling is a traditional form of human-powered boat propulsion in which a single oar is oscillated laterally at the stern. In this study, we investigate this propulsion technique from a hydrodynamic perspective by continuously measuring the oar kinematics, the boat motion, and the forces acting on the oar across a broad range of boat speeds. During the lateral strokes, lift serves as the main propulsive force, whereas during the backward strokes, propulsion is primarily associated with added-mass effects. These measurements allow us to determine the propulsive efficiency as a function of boat speed. The efficiency peaks at approximately 65\% at an intermediate speed and then decreases progressively to approximately 25\% at higher speeds. These results provide insight into the hydrodynamic mechanisms governing this traditional mode of propulsion and highlight the effectiveness of stern-sculling at moderate speeds.

infographic.key_insight: Stern-sculling propulsion relies mainly on lift during lateral strokes and added-mass effects during backward strokes, with peak efficiency near 65% at intermediate boat speed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These findings can inform oscillating-oar propulsion designs and operating speeds for efficient human-powered boats.
method: Continuously measure oar kinematics and boat motion.
Measure forces acting on the oar across a broad range of boat speeds.
Determine propulsive efficiency as a function of boat speed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Measurements show efficiency peaking at approximately 65% at intermediate speed and declining to approximately 25% at higher speeds.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract describes experimental measurements, not an AI or CFD surrogate, and does not establish generalizability across oar geometries or operators.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrodynamics and propulsive efficiency of stern-sculling propulsion
